newsitem.title: USA: Ford launches flexible fuel vehicle program.
newsitem.headline: Ford launches flexible fuel vehicle program.

text.p: Ford Motor Co. unveiled plans Tuesday to make 250,000 Ranger compact pickup trucks, Windstar minivans and Taurus sedans with flexible fuel engines that allow them to run on both ethanol and gasoline.

The new flexible fuel vehicle (FFV) programme will be phased in over a three- to four-year period, starting in the fall of 1998 with between 50,000 and 60,000 Ranger pickup trucks. FFV technology will be offered as standard equipment on Rangers equipped with 3.0-litre V-6 engines.
Ford will later expand the programme to include volume production of the Taurus and Windstar with the same V-6 engine.

Ford's cost to convert engines into FFV technology would be about $300 a vehicle, or $75 million for all 250,000 expected vehicles, Mike McCabe, marketing manager for worldwide alternative fuel vehicles, said at a new product briefing at Ford's proving grounds.
However, the total cost may be less than that as volumes increase and other cost savings are realised. Consumers will not bear the cost of the conversion, Ford officials said.
"We want this experience for the consumer to be totally transparent," said McCabe.

Ford already sells limited numbers of FFV versions of the Taurus to fleet customers. The vehicles run on methanol and ethanol. Since the Clean Air Act was passed in 1990, it has sold 12,117 FFVs, accounting for more than half of the 23,232 FFVs sold by the whole industry in that period.

Ford officials said the new vehicles are targeted at mainstream buyers. They are also designed to encourage an increase in the approximately 40 service stations that sell what is called E85, an 85 percent blend of ethanol and 15 percent gasoline.
"This is a general product for all consumers, not just fleets. This is for you and me," said McCabe.

But one analyst noted Ford gets federal credits for offering alternative fuel vehicles. The credits can be used to raise the company's corporate average fuel economy (CAFE), which the federal government sets to force automakers to offer a certain number of fuel efficient vehicles.
Such credits can be crucial to an automaker like Ford, which makes most of its money by selling gas-guzzling pickup trucks and sport utility vehicles.

"This is an attempt to help meet CAFE standards while still selling the same basic mixture of products in its fleet," said Michael Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting, a Farmington Hills, Mich., consulting firm.
In addition to beating Ford to market, Chrysler Corp. will get the same CAFE benefit when it offers a flexible fuel minivan for the 1998 model year, which starts this September, Robinet said.

Chrysler spokeswoman Michele Tinson said an announcement is planned for the next couple of weeks. She declined to comment further. General Motors Corp. has considered a similar programme but so far has not made a final decision, said Robinet.
Clean-burning ethanol, commonly produced by wet milling of corn and other grains, is used by most major oil companies to boost the octane in gasoline.

E85 costs about 10 percent less at the pump and generates slightly more accelerating power than gasoline. But because it has about 25 percent less energy density than gasoline, vehicles powered by E85 get fewer miles per gallon. The end result, said McCabe at Ford, is about a 15 percent cost penalty, something Ford believes consumers can live with.
